statements.text: Tech and innovation cannot outpace safety and common sense. We need to reassert control over rogue AI models before it’s too late.

The Department of Defense (DoD) must effectively leverage artificial intelligence (AI) to successfully meet the challenges of the future, so in the FY24 budget request we are investing $1.8 billion in AI.
statements.context: Exchange during the House Armed Services Committee hearing on the FY2024 Defense Department budget request.

statements.text: What are the key enablers and roadblocks to solving the data problem at the Department of Defense so we can stay competitive with our adversaries in this new domain? General Milley. The Department is focused on meeting the foundational data needs critical to achieving dynamic, near real time data sharing for decision-making, both with and without the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI).
statements.context: House Armed Services Committee hearing on the FY 2024 Defense Budget Request, with a question from Mr. Kim and response from General Milley.

statements.text: Thank you. In Executive Order 14110, the Biden Administration compels private industry to provide information on its development of artificial intelligence products. That order makes a seemingly novel use of DPA's Title VII, a compulsory information-gathering authority applied to an industry that has not otherwise been subject to DPA actions under either Title I or Title III. Has the DPA been used this way before, and if so, how often has it been used? Who wants to answer that?
statements.context: House hearing on Defense Production Act reauthorization focused on national security.

statements.text: I want to continue on that track on how AI can be leveraged to fight criminal activity. [...] can you talk about how hard it would be to identify millions of data points that identify criminal activity without the use of AI?
statements.context: Question posed during a congressional hearing on AI applications in financial services and housing.

statements.text: How is AI being deployed in the payments industry to detect fraudulent payments or any other nefarious activities?
statements.context: Mrs. Kim asks a question during a hearing titled 'AI Innovation Explored: Insights into AI Applications in Financial Services and Housing.'

statements.text: advancements in AI have created a lot of potential, but there are also a lot of fears about how AI will change how we interact with one another and conduct our work. [...] One of the issues raised in our Working Group discussion was the issue of AI explainability. [...] So can you touch on how you are meeting those core principles on explainability and addressing the black box issue?
statements.context: Congressional hearing on AI applications in financial services and housing, where Rep. Kim questions an industry witness after opening remarks.

statements.text: with, you know, the advent of AI and other technologies that are out there, I guess I just wanted to get a sense from you—you know, as you are seeing this across your portfolio, where are we heading here in terms of the capacity for AI to be used in those nefarious ways?
statements.context: Senate committee hearing on consumer protection, protecting workers' money, and the dignity of work.

statements.text: Are there any particular industries and sectors where you think that AI and next generation technologies can get to a place where they are replacing and displacing workers?
statements.context: Senate confirmation hearing for Keith Sonderling as Deputy Secretary of Labor.

statements.text: I guess I just wanted to ask you more specifically, what role do you think the Federal Government can and should play when it comes to AI regulation as we're worried in a bipartisan way about job loss and replacement, not augmentation of work, but replacement.
statements.context: Senate confirmation hearing for Keith Sonderling's nomination as Deputy Secretary of Labor.

statements.text: Is that the right framing of the race? Is it about the adoption internationally in terms of other countries? I guess I am trying to think through it. Like, part of what you just said in your previous response was that we want other nations to be able to build upon the U.S. AI stack. Is that the right framework? [...] Or is it more about the consumer? Is it more about getting the rest of the world and the 78 percent of the population to adopt AI applications that are U.S.?
statements.context: Senate hearing where Senator Kim questions an industry witness on the strategic framework for the U.S. AI race.

statements.text: I guess I just wanted to ask you to tease that out some more in terms of understanding what role we could play in Congress, in government, in terms of trying to accelerate and champion that AI adoption internationally?
statements.context: Senate hearing titled "Winning the AI Race: Strengthening U.S. Capabilities in Computing and Innovation," where Senator Kim questions a witness about international AI adoption.

statements.text: Congress passed the DPA to mobilize the country’s economic and industrial resources to respond to emergencies and protect our national security, not to give Donald Trump and Pete Hegseth tools to extort American companies that refuse to help the Pentagon to surveil Americans or build killer robots.
statements.venue: Joint statement with Sen. Warren, Senate Banking Committee minority

statements.text: I just signed up for Claude as I respect Anthropic for putting responsible use above profit. Hegseth refuses to agree that AI shouldn’t be used for mass surveillance of Americans and for creating robots authorized to kill without a human decision-maker. This is an incredibly important debate and I urge everyone, including other AI/tech companies, to call for responsible use.

I hope Artemis teaches us that it’s ok to not know everything immediately. Not only is that ok, we need that push to dig deeper. We should not think the limits of AI output is the limit of our knowledge, but instead build on tech to go even further. Artemis is the physical manifestation of that partnership between tech and humanity to explore and reignite a drive to find answers to questions we didn’t know to ask.

That humility is refreshing and rekindles something that we often lose in this modern moment — curiosity and exploration. What does exploration mean in the age of AI that can answer nearly any question at any time? Our tech has often led us to feel hubris, as if there isn’t anything unknowable that we can learn instantaneously.

Thank you. I want to put in one more point over here. On April 4, The Washington Post reported that Chinese AI firms with direct links to the PLA are using AI to analyze and publish intelligence on U.S. military positions in the Middle East. Even more alarming, Chinese companies have supplied the Houthis with satellite imagery and precision targeting data to strike U.S. and allied shipping in the Red Sea. So let me ask you, Mr. Mahmood, how should Congress think about the fact that China's AI ambitions are not just a bilateral technology competition and that they are already actively fueling conflicts involving China's partners like Iran?
statements.context: Congressional hearing on China's efforts to undermine U.S. AI leadership, featuring a question from Rep. Kim to a witness.

statements.text: Thank you, Chairman Moolenaar. [...] there are some who argue that despite efforts to slow China down, China's chip and AI companies appear to be accelerating progress. [...] So what is your assessment of these arguments?
statements.context: Mrs. Kim questions witnesses at a hearing on China's campaign to steal America's AI edge.

statements.text: AI is moving faster than anyone – including its creators – can understand or control. We need to act and act now to ensure that humans remain in control of this technology and that all people – not just the elite few – benefit from it.
statements.venue: Press release statement, Senator Kim's website

statements.text: Technology and innovation must move forward; it’s what has powered our nation’s economy and kept us safe. But moving forward recklessly without sensible controls is a recipe for chaos and danger. The American people don’t want this technology to advance without rules that they have a say in writing.
statements.venue: Press release statement, Senator Kim's website

statements.text: We really need a very specific regulatory framework when it comes to AI
statements.venue: Phone interview with Blue Light News

statements.text: Those are not mutually exclusive. And I think that comment by Trump was wrong. We can find bipartisan support to show that there is a real and better way that we can do this.
statements.venue: Phone interview with Blue Light News, on AI regulation and competition with China

statements.text: Innovation without control just leads to chaos, and this is our moment to make sure that the American people have control over the incredible strides we’re seeing on AI. Control means making sure that the technology does not outpace safety and common sense. It means making sure it can be used to advance quality of life instead of hurdling us towards the doomsday scenarios we’ve been warned about.
statements.venue: Press release on AI safety bill introduction with Warner and Schatz

statements.text: We should not be giving China the tools to make their own chips indigenously. Every time China has been able to make something at home, they have been able to make it bigger and cheaper than pretty much everyone in the world.
What I hate so much is just a lack of any transparency to the local communities.
statements.venue: NJ Spotlight News interview, on data centers

statements.text: We know that AI is moving incredibly fast. All of us in the Senate want to see us driving the innovation of the future. All of us want to see American businesses being able to be in the lead and pushing that forward. But the idea and the value of innovation and American technology pushing that frontier is not mutually exclusive with ensuring safety and security for the American people. Our job here is to make sure that we can have both happen.
statements.venue: Senate HSGAC subcommittee hearing on rogue AI, opening remarks

statements.text: We can’t wait any longer before we really push deeper into this conversation here in the Capitol…I say that as someone who worked in national security before, ensuring that we have that accurate information of what we’re dealing with.
statements.venue: Senate HSGAC subcommittee hearing on rogue AI
